chapter_title: Introduction to Ethernet Switching and VLANs
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the core of enterprise networking: Ethernet switching and the power of VLANs. At its heart, an Ethernet switch operates by learning the Media Access Control (MAC) addresses of devices connected to its ports. When a frame arrives on a port, the switch inspects the source MAC address and records it in its MAC address table, associating that MAC with the incoming port. This process, known as MAC address learning, allows the switch to intelligently forward subsequent frames destined for that MAC address only out the specific port where the device resides, rather than broadcasting it to all ports. If a destination MAC is unknown, the switch floods the frame out all ports (except the ingress port) within the same broadcast domain, hoping the destination will respond and reveal its location. This intelligent forwarding significantly improves network efficiency compared to older hub-based networks.

However, in larger networks, relying solely on physical segmentation or a single large broadcast domain can lead to significant problems. Every device in a single broadcast domain receives all broadcast traffic, which can include ARP requests, DHCP requests, and various service advertisements. As the number of devices grows, the volume of broadcast traffic increases, consuming bandwidth and CPU cycles on end devices and switches, leading to what's known as a "broadcast storm." Furthermore, a flat network offers minimal security; any device can potentially communicate with any other device, making it easier for attackers to snoop on traffic or move laterally across the network.

This is where Virtual Local Area Networks, or VLANs, become indispensable. A VLAN allows you to logically segment a single physical switch (or multiple interconnected switches) into several distinct broadcast domains. Devices within the same VLAN can communicate as if they were on the same physical segment, while devices in different VLANs require a Layer 3 device (like a router or a Layer 3 switch) to communicate. The benefits are profound: VLANs enhance network security by isolating traffic, reduce the size of broadcast domains (improving network performance), simplify network management by grouping users or devices based on function rather than physical location, and provide flexibility for network reorganization without physical recabling.

To implement VLANs, we use the IEEE 802.1Q standard, which defines a method for inserting a small tag (4 bytes) into the Ethernet frame header. This tag contains a VLAN ID (VID) that identifies which VLAN the frame belongs to. When a frame travels between switches or between a switch and a router, it often needs to carry information for multiple VLANs. This is where the concept of **trunk ports** comes in. A trunk port is configured to carry traffic for multiple VLANs, and it uses 802.1Q tagging to identify which VLAN each frame belongs to. Conversely, an **access port** is designed for end-user devices (like workstations, servers, or printers) and carries traffic for only a single VLAN. Traffic on an access port is typically *untagged* when it leaves the switch, as the end device is usually unaware of VLAN tags. The switch itself internally associates untagged frames received on an access port with its assigned VLAN.

A crucial aspect of trunk ports is the **native VLAN**. On an 802.1Q trunk, one VLAN can be designated as the native VLAN. Frames belonging to the native VLAN are sent *untagged* over the trunk. All other VLANs on the trunk are sent tagged. This can be a source of common mistakes: if the native VLAN is mismatched between two connected trunk ports, untagged traffic from one switch will be incorrectly assigned to a different VLAN on the other switch, leading to connectivity issues or even security vulnerabilities (known as VLAN hopping). Best practice often dictates explicitly tagging all VLANs on a trunk, or at least ensuring the native VLAN ID is consistent across connected devices and, ideally, an unused VLAN ID for security.

Let's look at the basic Junos OS commands to configure VLANs. First, you define the VLANs themselves, giving them a name and a VLAN ID. Then, you assign interfaces to these VLANs.

```junos
# Configure VLANs
set vlans VLAN_SALES vlan-id 10
set vlans VLAN_HR vlan-id 20
set vlans VLAN_SERVERS vlan-id 30

# Configure an access port for VLAN_SALES (VLAN ID 10)
# ge-0/0/0 is the interface connected to a sales workstation
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode access
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members VLAN_SALES

# Configure another access port for VLAN_HR (VLAN ID 20)
# ge-0/0/1 is the interface connected to an HR workstation
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode access
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members VLAN_HR

# Configure a trunk port to connect to another switch, carrying all configured VLANs
# ge-0/0/2 is the uplink to another switch
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode trunk
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [ VLAN_SALES VLAN_HR VLAN_SERVERS ]

# Alternatively, to allow all VLANs on the trunk (if you have many)
# set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members all

# Commit the changes
commit
```
After committing, you can verify your configuration using `show vlans` and `show interfaces ge-0/0/X extensive`. Understanding these foundational concepts of Ethernet switching and VLANs is critical for building robust, secure, and efficient enterprise networks. Always double-check your VLAN assignments and trunk configurations, especially the native VLAN, to prevent common connectivity issues.

screens.title: Introduction to Ethernet Switching and VLANs
screens.subtitle: How switches learn MACs, why broadcast domains matter, and how VLANs provide logical segmentation

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter we explore the core ideas that make modern enterprise switching work: MAC address learning, broadcast domains, and Virtual Local Area Networks. You'll learn how a switch builds a table of device locations from frame sources, how unknown destinations trigger flooding, and why a single flat broadcast domain becomes inefficient and risky as a network grows. VLANs let you partition a physical network into multiple logical segments, improving performance and security by reducing broadcast scope and grouping devices by role instead of by cable. We'll also cover 802.1Q tagging, the difference between access and trunk ports, the role of a native VLAN, and the basic Junos commands to create VLANs and assign interfaces on an EX series switch. Along the way you'll see common mistakes to avoid, such as mismatched native VLANs or incomplete trunk membership. A short hands-on scenario at the end guides you through creating two VLANs, assigning access ports, and configuring a trunk. By the end you'll be able to explain why VLANs are used and perform basic VLAN configuration with Junos commands. Think about a simple office where printers, servers, and guest laptops must be separated — VLANs let you do that without recabling. What problem would you solve first in your own network?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: VLANs and MAC learning are the foundation of scalable, secure Ethernet switching. Mastering them reduces broadcast traffic, isolates groups, and prevents common connectivity issues.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this lesson we set clear, assessable goals. First, you will understand how a switch learns and uses MAC addresses to forward frames efficiently. That means being able to describe the MAC learning process and explain why unknown destinations cause flooding. Second, you will explain VLAN purpose and benefits, such as reducing broadcast domains and grouping devices by function for easier administration and improved security. Each objective ties to practical tasks: verifying MAC learning tables, interpreting flood behavior, and mapping users into VLANs. Third, you will differentiate access and trunk ports, including when frames are tagged and when they are not. This is essential to avoid misconfigurations that break connectivity. Fourth, you will configure basic VLANs on a Juniper EX switch and assign access and trunk interfaces. That includes using set vlans, setting interface-mode to access or trunk, and verifying your work with show commands. Each objective is measurable: you should be able to run the commands, read outputs, and troubleshoot a mismatched VLAN on a trunk link. Consider which objective matters most in your current environment and focus there first.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Avoid Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Skills, mnemonics, and common pitfalls to watch for

narration.text: This page expands the objectives with practical context and simple mnemonics. First, when you learn MAC address behavior, remember the phrase 'Source builds the map, destination uses it.' Practically, that means when a device sends traffic, the switch records its MAC and port; later, the switch forwards frames to that port rather than flooding. Second, for VLANs, use the mnemonic 'Group by role, not by cable.' This helps you decide which users belong in each VLAN. Third, for ports, remember: access equals single VLAN and untagged to the end host; trunk equals multiple VLANs and 802.1Q tags across links between switches. Fourth, for configuration and verification, follow a simple checklist: define VLANs, set interface-mode, assign members, commit, and then run show vlans and show interfaces extensive. Also, be wary of native VLAN mismatches — treat native VLAN as a special case and align IDs on both sides or avoid relying on untagged frames. Each objective links to hands-on practice: configure, commit, and then validate with show commands to make this real.

screens.title: MAC Address Learning
screens.subtitle: How switches build the MAC address table and use it to forward frames

narration.text: Let's define MAC address learning clearly. A switch examines the source MAC address of each incoming Ethernet frame and records an association between that MAC and the physical port the frame arrived on. This entry goes into the switch's MAC address table. The switch uses that table to forward frames: when a frame arrives with a known destination MAC, the switch sends it only out the port recorded for that destination. If the destination is unknown, the switch floods the frame to all ports in the same broadcast domain except the ingress port, hoping the destination responds. A concrete example: when a PC boots and sends DHCP or ARP, those frames let the switch learn the PC's MAC and port. One common misconception is thinking the switch learns destination MACs — it does not; it learns sources and later applies that knowledge to destinations. Another mistake is assuming MAC entries are permanent — they age out and are refreshed by traffic. Practical significance: understanding this explains why a newly connected device triggers flooding until the switch learns its MAC and why clearing MAC tables or aging can temporarily increase broadcasts. Reflect: when you see unexpected flooding, what recent changes might have cleared or prevented MAC learning?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Switches learn source MACs and map them to ports; unknown destinations are flooded until learned.

content.html:
Core Concept MAC Address Learning
How a switch learns MACs
The switch records source MACs and associated ingress ports. The MAC table drives selective forwarding and limits unnecessary traffic.
Process explained
  • Inspect source MAC on every received frame and record port↔MAC mapping.
  • Use table entries to forward frames only to the port where the destination resides.
  • If destination unknown, flood within the broadcast domain until response builds the table.
  • MAC entries age out and are refreshed by traffic from the same device.
Example
A workstation sends ARP after boot. The switch learns the workstation's MAC from that ARP and records its port.
Common mistake
Assuming switches learn destination MACs or that entries never expire. Both lead to incorrect troubleshooting steps.
Visual: MAC table (annotated)
A compact table shows columns: VLAN, MAC address, Port, Age. Watching this table while devices start up illustrates learning in real time.
VLAN MAC Address Port Age 10 aa:bb:cc:11:22:33 ge-0/0/0 00:05 10 aa:bb:cc:44:55:66 ge-0/0/1 00:02
Key Takeaway

MAC learning is reactive: traffic from a device creates the table entry you then rely on for efficient forwarding.

screens.title: Forwarding and Flooding Behavior
screens.subtitle: What happens when a switch knows a MAC and when it does not

narration.text: Understanding forwarding versus flooding clarifies many troubleshooting scenarios. When a frame arrives, the switch checks the destination MAC in its MAC table. If an entry exists, the switch forwards the frame only to the recorded port. This is efficient and reduces unnecessary traffic. If no entry exists, the switch floods the frame to all ports in the same broadcast domain except where the frame came from. Flooding is a temporary mechanism that solicits a reply so the switch can learn the destination's source MAC. A concrete example: imagine a newly connected IP phone trying to reach a call server. The initial packets may flood until the server or phone responds; then the switch learns both MACs and subsequent packets are forwarded directly. A common misconception is that flooding always indicates a broken switch — rather, it's expected behavior for unknown destinations or when entries have aged out. Practical troubleshooting steps: capture traffic to see ARP or DHCP that triggers learning, check MAC table entries with show ethernet-switching table, and monitor entry age. Reflect: after learning occurs, does traffic stay stable or do entries continually age out in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Forward vs Flood
keyIdea.text: Known destination = selective forwarding. Unknown destination = flooding until the switch learns the MAC.

content.html:
Process Flow Forwarding and Flooding
Forward or Flood
A simple decision tree determines selective forwarding or broadcast flooding until learning occurs.
  1. Frame arrives; switch reads source MAC and updates table.
  2. Switch looks up destination MAC in the table.
  3. If found, forward to that port only.
  4. If not found, flood to all ports in the same VLAN except ingress.
  5. When destination replies, the switch learns its MAC and future frames are forwarded selectively.
Concrete example
A new printer sends ARP; initial frames flood. Once the printer responds, its MAC is recorded and normal forwarding resumes.
Misconception
Flooding is not always a fault. It is part of correct switch behavior for unknown destinations.
Annotated decision diagram
A compact diagram labels the check: update source → lookup destination → forward or flood. Use it to explain observed traffic patterns to peers.
Known destination
Forward only
Unknown destination
Flood then learn
Pro tip

When troubleshooting intermittent loss, check for MAC table flaps or rapid aging that can cause repeated flooding.

screens.title: Broadcast Domains and Why Flat Networks Fail
screens.subtitle: How broadcast traffic scales and the risks of large broadcast domains

narration.text: A broadcast domain is a logical network segment where every device receives broadcast traffic like ARP requests or DHCP discovery messages. In a small network this is fine, but as the number of devices grows, broadcast volume increases and consumes bandwidth and C P U resources on hosts and switches. This can lead to degraded performance or 'broadcast storms' when excessive broadcasts swamp the network. Another concern is security: in a flat broadcast domain, any device can reach any other at Layer 2, making lateral movement by an attacker easier. VLANs address both problems by creating multiple, smaller broadcast domains inside the same physical infrastructure. Each VLAN confines broadcasts to its members, reducing unnecessary traffic and limiting the scope of potential attacks. A practical example: place printers and guest devices in separate VLANs so their broadcast traffic doesn't reach sensitive servers. A common misconception is that VLANs increase performance by speeding links — instead they reduce unnecessary traffic on those links and therefore improve overall efficiency. Think about which groups of devices in your environment generate frequent broadcasts and how you might isolate them with VLANs.

keyIdea.title: Broadcast domain
keyIdea.text: A broadcast domain groups devices that receive each other's broadcast traffic; VLANs split large domains into smaller, manageable ones.

content.html:
Definition Broadcast Domain
What a broadcast domain is
Devices in the same broadcast domain receive each other's broadcast traffic such as ARP and DHCP messages.
Why large broadcast domains fail
  • Broadcast volume grows with device count and consumes bandwidth.
  • End systems and switches spend CPU processing irrelevant broadcasts.
  • Security risk: easy lateral movement when all devices see the same Layer 2 traffic.
Analogy
Think of a broadcast domain as a room where everyone hears every announcement. Too many people makes announcements ineffective and noisy.
How VLANs mitigate the problem
By splitting the physical network into VLANs, broadcasts are contained and only reach VLAN members, saving bandwidth and improving security.
Server VLAN
Isolated, low broadcast noise
Guest VLAN
Contains noisy devices
Key Takeaway

Use VLANs to limit broadcast reach, reduce unnecessary processing, and improve segmentation for security.

screens.title: What is a VLAN?
screens.subtitle: Logical grouping of devices and the benefits VLANs provide

narration.text: A VLAN, or Virtual Local Area Network, is a logical grouping of network devices that behave as if they are on the same physical segment, even if they are spread across multiple switches. VLANs create separate broadcast domains on the same physical switch infrastructure. Practical benefits include improved security through isolation, reduced broadcast traffic by limiting domain size, and administrative flexibility: you can group devices by role — for example, servers, finance, and guest devices — without moving cables. A concrete scenario: placing all servers in VLAN 30 prevents noisy user broadcasts from reaching critical systems and allows you to apply consistent firewall or ACL rules. A common misconception is that VLANs change IP addressing automatically — they do not. VLANs define Layer 2 separation; inter-VLAN communication still requires a Layer 3 device or routed interface. When planning VLANs, consider traffic patterns, security zones, and how you will route between VLANs. A reflective question: which groups in your environment should be isolated at Layer 2 and why? What is a VLAN? means a vlan is a logical broadcast domain that groups devices by role to improve security and reduce broadcast scope.. In practical terms, logical grouping of devices and the benefits vlans provide. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: VLAN definition
keyIdea.text: A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain that groups devices by role to improve security and reduce broadcast scope.

content.html:
Definition VLAN (Virtual LAN)
VLANs let you group devices logically
They create distinct broadcast domains without requiring separate physical switches for each group.
Common uses
  • Isolate servers from user workstations.
  • Separate guest Wi-Fi from internal networks.
  • Group voice devices into a dedicated VLAN for QoS and policy.
Misconception
VLANs do not route traffic between each other; routing requires a Layer 3 device or interface.
Example VLAN layout
VLAN 10: Users, VLAN 20: Voice, VLAN 30: Servers. Each VLAN confines broadcasts and can receive tailored policies.
Key Takeaway

Design VLANs around roles and traffic patterns to minimize broadcast reach and simplify policy application.

screens.title: 802.1Q VLAN Tagging
screens.subtitle: How a 4-byte 802.1Q tag identifies VLAN membership across links

narration.text: The IEEE 802.1Q standard defines how VLAN membership is carried inside Ethernet frames as they travel across network links. Specifically, a 4-byte tag is inserted into the Ethernet header containing the VLAN ID. This tag tells intermediate switches and routers which VLAN the frame belongs to. On links that carry multiple VLANs — trunks — most VLAN frames are sent with this 802.1Q tag. A key detail is the native VLAN: frames for that VLAN may be sent untagged across the trunk. A concrete example: when a frame belonging to VLAN 10 traverses an inter-switch trunk, it carries the VLAN 10 tag so the receiving switch can associate the frame with VLAN 10 and forward it only to ports in that VLAN. A common mistake is assuming endpoints see tags on access ports — they do not. Access ports remove or add tags at the edge so end devices typically see untagged frames. Another operational note: misconfigured tagging or inconsistent native VLANs on two sides of a trunk leads to VLAN misassignment and potential security issues. Consider a trunk link carrying voice and data: tagging keeps traffic separated while sharing the physical link. How will you ensure consistent tagging across your trunk links?

keyIdea.title: 802.1Q tag
keyIdea.text: A 4-byte 802.1Q tag in the Ethernet header carries the VLAN ID so frames remain associated with the correct VLAN across trunks.

content.html:
Architecture 802.1Q Tagging
How tagging preserves VLAN identity
802.1Q inserts a small tag with the VLAN ID into the Ethernet header so frames can traverse shared links without losing VLAN context.
Key facts
  • The tag is 4 bytes and includes the VLAN ID.
  • Trunks carry tagged frames for most VLANs and may send native VLAN frames untagged.
  • Access ports present untagged frames to end devices and map them to a single VLAN internally.
Mistake to avoid
Mismatched native VLAN IDs on trunk endpoints cause untagged frames to be misclassified and can create connectivity or security problems.
Example packet annotation
An Ethernet frame with an 802.1Q tag shows source, destination, and VLAN ID fields. This ID follows through the network to keep frames in the correct domain.
[ Eth Dest ][ Eth Src ][ 802.1Q Tag: VLAN 10 ][ Eth Type ][ Payload ]
Why it matters

Tags keep multiple VLANs separate on a single physical link, enabling flexible and efficient use of infrastructure.

screens.title: Access Port vs Trunk Port
screens.subtitle: When to use access ports and when to use trunks

narration.text: Differentiating access and trunk ports is fundamental. An access port is intended for a single end device or a small set of devices and carries traffic for only one VLAN. Traffic leaving an access port toward an end device is typically untagged since most hosts do not understand 802.1Q tags. In practice, you configure user workstations, servers that are in a single VLAN, and printers on access ports. A trunk port, by contrast, carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches or to routers. Trunks use 802.1Q tags so frames for VLANs other than the native VLAN are labeled and properly routed on the receiving side. A concrete example: connect a workstation to ge-0/0/0 as an access port for VLAN 10 so its traffic is untagged to the host. Use ge-0/0/2 as a trunk uplink carrying VLANs 10, 20, and 30 to the next switch. A common misconception is configuring server-facing ports as trunks by default; unless a server expects tagged interfaces, this will break connectivity. Closing question: for a multi-VLAN wireless access point that terminates several SSIDs, which port type do you choose and why?

keyIdea.title: Access vs Trunk
keyIdea.text: Access ports serve one VLAN and are untagged to hosts; trunk ports carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tagging between network devices.

content.html:
Comparison Access Port vs Trunk Port
Choose the right port type
Match interface mode to the device's VLAN awareness and the intended traffic separation.
Access port
  • Single VLAN membership, untagged to the end host.
  • Used for workstations, single-VLAN servers, and printers.
  • Configured with interface-mode access and vlan members.
Trunk port
  • Carries multiple VLANs between switches or to routers.
  • Uses 802.1Q tagging for non-native VLANs.
  • Configured with interface-mode trunk and a list of vlan members.
Concrete examples
Access: ge-0/0/0 connected to a desktop in VLAN 10. Trunk: ge-0/0/2 uplink carrying VLANs 10, 20, 30 to other switches.
Common mistake
Using trunk mode for endpoints that do not understand tags will prevent connectivity because the host will receive tagged frames.
Key Takeaway

Match port mode to device capability: untagged access for hosts, tagged trunks for multi-VLAN links.

screens.title: Native VLANs and Mismatch Risks
screens.subtitle: Why native VLANs exist and how mismatches cause misclassification

narration.text: A native VLAN is a VLAN on a trunk link whose frames are sent untagged. Historically, this accommodated devices or links that did not add or expect tags. Operationally, a trunk carries tagged frames for most VLANs and sends native VLAN frames without tags. The key risk arises when the native VLAN is different on the two ends of a trunk. Untagged frames arriving at the peer will be assigned to that peer's native VLAN, which could be a different VLAN ID. The result is misclassified traffic that appears in the wrong VLAN and can cause connectivity failures or security exposure. A concrete example: trunk A has native VLAN 1 while trunk B uses native VLAN 99. Untagged traffic sent from A will be treated as VLAN 99 by B, causing devices to be placed in the wrong broadcast domain. A common mitigation is to explicitly tag all VLANs and align native VLAN IDs across connected devices or use an unused VLAN ID for native traffic to reduce attack surface. For troubleshooting, check trunk configurations on both sides and confirm the vlan members and any native-vlan settings. Reflect: would you prefer to tag every VLAN or rely on native VLANs in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Native VLAN caution
keyIdea.text: Native VLANs send untagged frames; mismatches between trunk endpoints can misclassify traffic and lead to connectivity or security problems.

content.html:
Process Flow Native VLAN
Native VLAN behavior
Frames for the native VLAN may be sent untagged across an 802.1Q trunk. That makes consistent configuration critical.
Consequences of mismatch
  • Untagged frames assigned to the wrong VLAN on the receiving switch.
  • Connectivity problems or unintended communication between hosts.
  • Potential security exposure via VLAN hopping if untagged traffic is mishandled.
Mitigation
Either tag all VLANs across the trunk, or explicitly align native VLAN IDs and use an unused VLAN for native traffic.
Example mismatch scenario
Switch A native VLAN = 1, Switch B native VLAN = 99. Untagged frames from A appear in VLAN 99 on B, causing hosts to be placed incorrectly.
Common mistake

Relying on default native VLAN IDs without verifying both sides of a trunk is a frequent source of misconfiguration.

screens.title: Junos VLAN Configuration Basics
screens.subtitle: Defining VLANs and the basic set commands

narration.text: Now we'll look at the basic Junos commands to define VLANs on an EX series switch. Start in configuration mode, create a named VLAN and assign a numeric VLAN ID. These VLAN definitions are logical objects you can reference when assigning interfaces. The next step is setting interface-mode on physical interfaces to access or trunk and listing the vlan members for each. A concrete example from the chapter: defining VLAN_SALES with vlan-id 10 and assigning ge-0/0/0 as an access port member of VLAN_SALES. A common troubleshooting point is forgetting to add VLAN members on a trunk — if you configure an uplink as a trunk on one switch and don't list the same VLANs on the remote switch, traffic for missing VLANs will be dropped. After configuring, commit and verify using show vlans and show interfaces extensive to confirm member lists and operational state. When you type the commands, think of them as building blocks: define VLANs, set interface modes, assign members, then commit and verify. Which verification command will you run first after committing? Junos VLAN Configuration Basics means define vlans, set interface-mode to access or trunk, assign vlan members, commit, then verify with show commands.. In practical terms, defining vlans and the basic set commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Junos config steps
keyIdea.text: Define VLANS, set interface-mode to access or trunk, assign vlan members, commit, then verify with show commands.

content.html:
Configuration Junos VLAN Commands
Define VLAN objects
VLANs are created as named objects with numeric IDs and referenced on interfaces.
Commands (example)
# Configure VLANs
set vlans VLAN_SALES vlan-id 10
set vlans VLAN_HR vlan-id 20
set vlans VLAN_SERVERS vlan-id 30

# Commit
commit
Verification
Use show vlans to list VLANs and show interfaces ge-0/0/X extensive to confirm interface mode and membership.
Practical note
Define all VLANs before assigning them to interfaces to avoid missing members on trunks. Be explicit about the VLAN list on uplinks to ensure consistency.
Key Takeaway

Junos uses named VLAN objects. Build them, assign interfaces, commit, then verify with show commands.

screens.title: Assigning Access Ports — Example
screens.subtitle: Configure ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 as access ports for different VLANs

narration.text: This walkthrough shows concrete commands to assign access ports to VLANs on a Juniper EX switch. First ensure the VLAN objects exist. Then set the interface to interface-mode access and list the VLAN object as a member. For example, ge-0/0/0 can be an access port in VLAN_IT with vlan-id 100, and ge-0/0/1 can be an access port in VLAN_GUEST with vlan-id 200. After committing, verify that each interface reports interface-mode access and that the VLAN membership is correct. A common troubleshooting sequence is to confirm the physical link is up, check the interface mode, and then inspect the MAC table to ensure the host appears under the expected VLAN. Misconceptions to avoid: assigning the wrong VLAN object name or forgetting to commit are frequent causes of apparent misconfiguration. Always run show vlans after commit and compare the interface outputs to ensure hosts are placed in the correct broadcast domain. Assigning Access Ports — Example means set interface-mode to access and add the vlan object as a member; commit and verify with show commands.. In practical terms, configure ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 as access ports for different vlans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access port assignment
keyIdea.text: Set interface-mode to access and add the VLAN object as a member; commit and verify with show commands.

content.html:
Configuration Access Port Example
Access port commands
Define VLAN objects, set the interface to access, and add the VLAN member.
# Define VLANs
set vlans VLAN_IT vlan-id 100
set vlans VLAN_GUEST vlan-id 200

# Configure access ports
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode access
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members VLAN_IT

set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode access
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members VLAN_GUEST

# commit
commit
Verification steps
  1. Run show vlans to confirm VLANs and members.
  2. Run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive to check interface-mode and VLAN assignment.
  3. Check the MAC table to ensure the host MAC appears under the correct VLAN and port.
Key Takeaway

Follow define→assign→commit→verify and confirm both VLAN and interface states to avoid access-port misassignments.

screens.title: Trunk Configuration and Verification
screens.subtitle: Configure a trunk to carry multiple VLANs and confirm consistent membership

narration.text: A trunk port allows multiple VLANs to traverse a single physical link using 802.1Q tags. To configure a trunk on Junos, set the interface-mode to trunk and list the VLAN members that should be allowed on that link. You can list specific VLANs or use the keyword all. A concrete example: configure ge-0/0/2 as an uplink carrying VLAN_IT and VLAN_GUEST. After committing, verify the trunk with show interfaces extensive to ensure the interface is in trunk mode and show vlans to confirm the remote membership. A common pitfall is asymmetric trunk configuration: if one side permits VLANs 10 and 20 and the other side permits only VLAN 10, traffic for VLAN 20 will be dropped. Another risk is mismatched native VLANs leading to untagged traffic misplacement. When troubleshooting, compare both sides of the uplink and check the MAC table for VLAN presence across the link. For lab practice, configure a trunk, ping across VLANs via a routed interface, and observe MAC learning across the uplink. Which show output will reveal dropped frames for an unexpected VLAN? Trunk Configuration and Verification means set interface-mode to trunk, list vlan members, commit, and verify that both ends have consistent vlan membership to avoid dropped traffic.. In practical terms, configure a trunk to carry multiple vlans and confirm consistent membership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trunk setup
keyIdea.text: Set interface-mode to trunk, list VLAN members, commit, and verify that both ends have consistent VLAN membership to avoid dropped traffic.

content.html:
Configuration & Verification Trunk Port
Trunk commands
Allow multiple VLANs on the uplink and verify both endpoints match.
# Configure trunk uplink
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode trunk
set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members [ VLAN_IT VLAN_GUEST ]

# Or allow all VLANs
# set interfaces ge-0/0/2 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members all

commit
Verification checklist
  • Run show vlans to confirm member lists on both switches.
  • Run show interfaces ge-0/0/2 extensive to confirm interface-mode is trunk.
  • Check MAC tables to see VLAN MACs learned across the uplink.
Common mistake

Inconsistent VLAN membership on trunk endpoints causes certain VLAN traffic to be dropped; verify both sides match.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas you should retain. First, MAC address learning: switches record source MACs and the ingress port to build a forwarding table. Second, broadcast domain: a VLAN defines which devices receive each other's broadcast traffic; reducing domain size lowers broadcast load. Third, VLAN: a logical grouping of devices that provides isolation, easier management, and the ability to apply policies by role. Keep these three concepts front of mind when designing or troubleshooting switch behavior. For each, a quick verification step helps: observe the MAC table for learning, check show vlans for broadcast domain membership, and review VLAN assignments to ensure devices are placed in the right logical groups. These checks translate directly into faster, more accurate troubleshooting. What small verification will you do first when you return to your lab?

keyIdea.text: MAC learning, broadcast domains, and VLANs are the essential building blocks of switched network design.

content.html:
What to Remember Key Concepts
MAC Address Learning
Switch learns source MACs and maps them to ports.
Broadcast Domain
Devices that see each other's broadcasts; VLANs limit this scope.
VLAN
Logical grouping of devices into separate broadcast domains.
Summary

These concepts explain why switches forward selectively, why VLANs matter for performance and security, and what to verify when problems occur.

narration.text: Finish with three operational reminders. First, 802.1Q defines the VLAN tagging mechanism that travels inside Ethernet frames; tagging keeps multi-VLAN traffic correct across trunks. Second, an access port is single-VLAN and typically sends untagged frames to end devices, so configure endpoints as access when they are not VLAN-aware. Third, a trunk port carries multiple VLANs and requires consistent VLAN membership on both ends to avoid dropped traffic. For daily operations, check show vlans to confirm definitions, show interfaces extensive to check interface-mode, and inspect the ethernet-switching table to see learned MACs and where traffic lives. These checks let you spot native VLAN mismatches, missing trunk members, and unexpected flooding. Keep these three checks as part of your routine when validating VLAN and switching behavior. Quick checklist
